messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi had always been drawn to a career in law enforcement, but nothing could have prepared him for the trauma he experienced during his first year as a detective. He was 18 when he was kidnapped by a suspect he had been investigating, held captive for three days in a cramped, dingy room with no windows. The only sounds were the muffled voices of his captors and the creaking of the old building. Kofi's mind racing with thoughts of escape, but his body was frozen in fear. When he was finally rescued, Kofi thought he had put the ordeal behind him. But as time passed, he began to notice that certain things triggered memories of those three days. The sound of footsteps outside his apartment at night would send his heart racing, and he would lie awake, convinced that someone was coming for him again. He started avoiding going out at night, opting instead to stay indoors, where it felt safer. Kofi also found himself recoiling from physical contact with others. A touch on the arm or a pat on the back would make him flinch, transporting him back to the feeling of being restrained and helpless. His girlfriend, Nia, noticed the change in him and tried to be understanding, but Kofi couldn't explain why he felt this way. He just knew that it made him feel vulnerable. When memories of his captivity did surface, Kofi struggled to put them into words. He would try to describe what happened, but the words wouldn't come. It was as if his brain had locked away the details, and he couldn't access them. But the sounds were still there, echoing in his mind - the creaks and groans of the old building, the muffled voices of his captors. Sometimes, Kofi would feel a wave of fear wash over him without any clear memory or image to explain it. It was as if his body remembered the trauma even when his mind didn't. He would be in the middle of a conversation with Nia or working on a case, and suddenly he would feel like he was back in that cramped room, fighting for air. As the months passed, Kofi's avoidance behaviors started to take a toll on his relationships and his work. His colleagues noticed that he was distant and preoccupied, and his performance began to suffer. Nia felt like she was losing him, like he was disappearing into himself. Kofi knew he needed help, but he didn't know where to start. One night, as he lay awake listening to the sounds outside his apartment, Kofi realized that he couldn't keep living like this. He needed to confront what had happened and find a way to heal. The thought of facing his memories head-on terrified him, but it also gave him a glimmer of hope. Maybe, just maybe, he could learn to live with what had happened and find a way to move forward. The next morning, Kofi made an appointment with a therapist, taking the first tentative step towards recovery. As he sat in the waiting room, he felt a sense of trepidation mixed with determination. He knew it wouldn't be easy, but he was ready to face whatever lay ahead, one small step at a time.
